title: What groceries cost in Germany
description: Typical prices for everyday food in Germany, what a student spends on groceries per month and the habits that keep the bill down.
html:
Germany is one of the cheaper Western European countries for groceries, mainly because discount supermarkets set the tone for the whole market. Most students spend between €150 and €250 a month on food if they cook at home. Here is what things cost and how people keep within that range.

Typical prices

These are rough supermarket prices in 2026; organic ranges and small shops cost more.

  • Bread, 500 g loaf: €1.50 to €3
  • Milk, 1 litre: €1.10 to €1.50
  • Eggs, 10: €2.50 to €3.50
  • Rice or pasta, 1 kg: €1.50 to €2.50
  • Chicken breast, 1 kg: €8 to €12
  • Tomatoes, 1 kg: €2.50 to €4
  • Apples, 1 kg: €2 to €3
  • Cheese, 200 g: €2 to €4
  • Coffee, 500 g: €5 to €8
  • Beer, 0.5 l bottle: €0.80 to €1.50

Eating out is where the money goes: a simple lunch costs €8 to €12, a restaurant dinner €15 to €25 without drinks. University canteens are the exception, with meals from €3 to €5 for students.

Where people shop

Discounters are the default for most households and carry everything from vegetables to detergent at the lowest prices. Full-range supermarkets have more brands and longer opening hours. Weekly markets are good for fresh produce and often cheaper than supermarkets late in the day. Asian, Turkish and Arabic grocers in every large city stock ingredients that mainstream supermarkets do not carry, usually at better prices.

Habits that keep the bill down

Buy store brands; the quality is generally the same as branded products. Watch for the weekly offers, which are printed in the leaflets and apps and can halve the price of meat and dairy. Cook in batches. Use the canteen for lunch. Return bottles: the deposit of 8 to 25 cents adds up. And remember that shops are closed on Sundays, so plan the weekend shop on Saturday.
